newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's DASA to spin off two plants to cut costs.
newsitem.headline: Germany's DASA to spin off two plants to cut costs.

text.p: Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA), Germany's largest aircraft maker, is spinning off two of its aircraft plants as part of a company-wide effort to reduce costs and return to profit by 1998, DASA said late on Saturday in a statement.

According to DASA, the aerospace unit of industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG, employees at its plant in Speyer will take over the works from January 1, 1997. A second plant in Laupheim will also leave DASA, but the company had no specific details on who the new owners would be.
The streamlining is part of DASA's rigorous cost-cutting programme, called Dolores, which was announced to widespread work stoppages and protests last autumn.

The Speyer plant will become a limited partnership under the ownership of its 550 workers from the start of the year, DASA said, adding only that Laupheim is preparing to be taken over by potential partners.
"I am delighted that we can prove to the whole world that Germany is internationally competitive at making aircraft," DASA chief Manfred Bischoff said in a statement.

DASA, which lost more than four billion marks ($2.7 billion) last year, announced it would hive off the two plants, slash its workforce, and cut overhead in an attempt to protect itself from swings in the currency market and from lower-cost producers such as Seattle-based Boeing Co.
Bischoff said the moves would strengthen DASA's position as a partner in the Airbus Industrie consortium, which is being transformed into a private company.
Erwin Hilbrink, chairman of DASA's works council, welcomed employee ownership at Speyer, saying the plant now had good prospects for the future.
DASA will help with the takeover at Speyer by offering the plant contracts at world prices for the first five years of its independence.
Hilbrink said that Speyer will probably reduce its work force by 100 to 450 by 1999 in order to reduce costs and be in a position to compete for those contracts. ($1=1.4793 Mark)
